I am 73 years old, and I have farmed these three *mu* of land in Quzhou County since I was a young man. My father and grandfather did the same before me. I only finished primary school, but the land has been my true teacher. Here on the North China Plain, the only thing that makes sense is what we have always done: winter wheat followed by summer maize, year after year. I sowed my wheat last October before the frost, and now that spring has arrived I can see it turning green. I will top-dress it with urea and irrigate it twice more—once at jointing and once at heading—before harvesting in early June. I never miss those timings. As soon as the wheat is threshed, I will plant hybrid maize the very same day. At my age I do not have the strength to plough deep anymore, so I will use no-tillage seeding straight into the wheat stubble. It saves time, saves diesel, and saves my back. I buy my seeds from the same agricultural supply shop in town every year—improved wheat and hybrid maize—because I know they will germinate well and the grain station will always buy the harvest. For fertilizer, I follow the amounts I have always used: plenty of nitrogen so the crop gets green and tall, some phosphorus to help the roots, and a little potash. I know roughly how many jin to spread. I will irrigate the maize two or three times through the summer, especially when the weather turns dry in July. If I see aphids or leaf blight coming, I will spray, but I will not waste money on chemicals when there is no pest. I do not experiment with vegetables or strange new crops for sale because the market is uncertain and my family depends on these two grains for both food and cash. If the weather stays fair, my wheat should give me about 500 kilograms per *mu*, and the maize a little more, maybe 550 kilograms per *mu*. That is enough for us.
